values.description: Assigning replica counts according to repository demand supports hundreds of replicas for busy monorepos and fewer replicas for small repositories.

values.label: Replica-count expansion for capacity
values.description: Increasing replicas as the primary way to scale massive repositories is rejected because synchronization latency and push throughput degrade.

values.label: Arbitrary replica expansion for read scaling
values.description: Deploying an arbitrary number of replicas to scale read throughput with replica count.

values.label: Linear read-throughput scaling
values.description: Read throughput increases linearly as replicas are added.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Commit Coordination
selected_clusters.description: Which coordination, locking, validation, and commit protocol establishes ordered and consistent updates across replicas.

relations.reading: Choices on Replica Commit Coordination affect the outcomes of Reference-State Integrity Verification
relations.rationale: The propagation and commit model determines when replicas can be compared and how much additional verification is needed to detect divergence.

values.label: Three-phase coordinated commit
values.description: Reference transactions use three-phase commit so replicas agree before a push is accepted.

values.label: Fully consistent replica cluster
values.description: Replicas remain mutually consistent for horizontally scalable reads and repository operations.

values.label: On-disk repository consensus source
values.description: Using healthy on-disk repository copies as the authoritative basis for consensus and push acceptance.

values.label: Atomic compare-and-swap WAL updates
values.description: Synchronizing concurrent WAL updates with atomic compare-and-swap.

values.label: Consensus-based repository primary election
values.description: Electing a repository primary through consensus before accepting updates.

values.label: Majority-replica exclusive write locking
values.description: Writes acquire exclusive locks on a replica majority to prevent conflicting concurrent updates.

values.label: Overlapped replica network waits
values.description: Useful locking, checksum, or database work runs while remote replica operations are pending.

values.label: Leaderless per-write voting
values.description: Selects each write’s winning order and outcome through replica voting without electing a single write-ordering primary.

values.label: Synchronous replica commitment
values.description: Acknowledges a write only after the required replicas have synchronously committed it durably.

values.label: Reference-value precondition validation
values.description: Validates expected old reference values and proposed new values before committing a coordinated reference transaction.

values.label: Pre-transaction local reference locking
values.description: Acquires all required local reference locks before validating and committing a coordinated update.

values.label: Deterministic cross-replica transaction results
values.description: Ensures coordinated reference transactions produce the same result on every participating replica.

values.label: Git reference update transactions
values.description: Represents Git reference changes as coordinated transactions that can commit or roll back across replicas.

values.label: Replica-count scaling under three-phase commit
values.description: Expanding the synchronized replica set is rejected because every coordination step waits for the slowest server.

values.label: S3-backed WAL synchronization and source of truth
values.description: Using S3-backed write-ahead logging for durable synchronization, validation, and authoritative repository state.

values.label: WAL-first replica synchronization
values.description: Repository updates enter a write-ahead log before replica synchronization, preserving durability while enabling horizontal scale.

values.label: Single-local-repository reference synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize with one local repository instead of coordinating a replica quorum.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Write Durability
selected_clusters.description: Which write-acceptance and durability guarantees determine when updates are acknowledged, refused, or preserved.

values.label: Globally consistent replica reads
values.description: S3 validation and catch-up produce a consistent repository view even when replication notifications are delayed or lost.

values.label: Low-latency replica communication requirement
values.description: Requiring nearby, low-latency proxy-to-replica communication to sustain high update rates.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
values.description: Fully synchronized replicas impose substantial architectural and operational complexity.

values.label: Push unavailability after quorum loss
values.description: Pushes cannot be accepted after too many healthy repository copies are lost.

values.label: Sub-three replica allocation
values.description: Reducing replicas below three for small repositories is rejected because it would weaken consistency and risk data loss.

values.label: Weaker durability and consistency guarantees
values.description: Relaxing hard durability or consistency guarantees to improve scaling or throughput.

values.label: Quorum-based push acceptance
values.description: Accepting pushes only while enough healthy replicas remain to form a quorum.

values.label: Durable push acknowledgement
values.description: A push is acknowledged only after its write-ahead-log entry is fully persisted.

values.label: Single-object-storage-write-per-push
values.description: Every push performs one object-storage write as its limiting persistence operation.

values.label: Single-extra-copy durability strategy
values.description: Keeping one extra copy provides single-node durability without majority coordination for conflicting writes.

values.label: All-or-nothing failed-write rollback
values.description: Reverts tentative or non-majority updates everywhere they were applied when validation or quorum agreement fails.

values.label: Write refusal during replica shortfall
values.description: Refuses writes when the minimum safe number of replica commitments cannot be achieved.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerance priority
values.description: Prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance over unrestricted availability in replica coordination.

values.label: Minimum two-replica write commitment
values.description: Requires every accepted write to be committed to at least two repository replicas.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Replication Mechanism
selected_clusters.description: How are repository data and mutation history propagated among hosting replicas?

values.label: Application-level repository replication
values.description: The hosting application replicates repository data without distributing or modifying Git itself.

values.label: Proxy-mediated multi-fileserver replication
values.description: Using a proxy as the coordination point that transparently replicates each push to multiple fileservers.

values.label: All-replica update replication
values.description: Replicating a Git update to every repository replica when possible.

values.label: Filesystem block-level replication
values.description: Replicating repository state through filesystem block-level mechanisms.

values.label: Combined Git and rsync replication
values.description: Repository copies are replicated, repaired, and rebalanced using both Git and rsync mechanisms.

values.label: External relational reference database
values.description: Repository references are stored in an external relational database alongside blob-stored packfiles.

values.label: WAL provenance for repository mutations
values.description: Pushes and repacks retain complete write-ahead-log history for diagnosing storage and Git failures.

values.label: Replica rewind and fast-forward from WAL history
values.description: Replicas rewind or fast-forward from recorded WAL history without external reference or object-database synchronization.

values.label: WAL-propagated compaction events
values.description: Records compaction results in the WAL so replicas apply the same repository and WAL compaction history.

selected_clusters.name: Reference-Update Publication Scheduling
selected_clusters.description: How are logical reference updates scheduled, batched, prioritized, and published to users?

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping-update transactions
values.description: Combining cascaded bookkeeping reference updates into fewer transactions.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: Prioritizing user-initiated reference updates over non-critical bookkeeping work.

values.label: WAL-indexed linearizable publication
values.description: Repository reference visibility follows successful reference preparation and WAL-index update.

values.label: Batched WAL ingestion
values.description: WAL entries are ingested in tuned batches rather than one object-storage write per push.

values.label: Read-preserving reference-update optimization
values.description: Reference-update optimizations improve write handling without degrading the much larger read workload.

values.label: Git reference-operation speedups
values.description: Optimizes individual Git reference operations to reduce coordinated update time.

values.label: Reduced user-request blocking
values.description: Fewer delays and timeouts caused by cascaded reference-update bookkeeping.

values.label: Distributed reference-update performance optimization
values.description: Optimized distributed reference updates support long-distance replication with improved robustness and speed.

values.label: Reference-update latency budget
values.description: Each reference update completes within a few hundred milliseconds to sustain practical per-repository update rates.

values.label: Reference-update workload amplification
values.description: One user action expands into many internal reference updates that the publication system must process.

values.label: Latency-limited reference-update throughput
values.description: Replica distance limits the sustainable rate of logical reference updates.

selected_clusters.name: Reference-State Integrity Verification
selected_clusters.description: The axis of variation is how systems detect divergence in logical Git references and sustain verification throughput for busy repositories.

values.label: Incremental XOR reference checksum
values.description: Reference-pair hashes are XOR-aggregated and updated in constant time when a reference changes.

values.label: From-scratch checksum recomputation
values.description: Recomputing checksums from every reference is rejected because its cost limits update throughput for repositories with many references.

values.label: Per-update checksum verification
values.description: A checksum is computed after each update to verify that replicas retain matching logical state.

values.label: Checksum-limited update throughput
values.description: Checksum computation cost constrains the maximum reference-update rate, especially for repositories with many references.

selected_clusters.name: Server Reboot and Failure Isolation
selected_clusters.description: How are servers quiesced, rebooted, retired, and isolated to preserve service redundancy?

relations.reading: Choices on Server Reboot and Failure Isolation affect the outcomes of Repository Replica Count
relations.rationale: Unexpected server loss temporarily reduces repository redundancy, while controlled maintenance limits simultaneous capacity and failure-domain reduction.

values.label: Controlled rolling reboots with quiescence and rack domains
values.description: Planned maintenance uses rolling, rack-scoped reboots, quiesces servers, excludes new reads, and preserves active work and redundancy.

values.label: Random chaos-monkey reboots
values.description: Random server reboots are rejected because they interrupt long-running reads.

values.label: Unplanned server unplugging
values.description: Unplugging servers without controlled retirement is rejected because it disrupts reads and unexpectedly reduces repository redundancy.

values.label: Continued write replication during quiescence
values.description: Continuing writes to a quiescing replica so it does not fall arbitrarily behind.

values.label: Temporary two-copy repository state
values.description: Sudden server loss leaves repositories with two copies, preserving immediate reads and writes but eliminating tolerance for another failure.

values.label: Rack-failure isolation
values.description: Preserving repository availability and durability when an entire rack fails.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Lifecycle and Repair
selected_clusters.description: How are idle replicas removed and damaged or incomplete repositories repaired and caught up?

values.label: Idle replica garbage collection
values.description: Removing inactive replicas from disk and rematerializing them from durable state reduces storage consumption without losing repository data.

values.label: Rapid repository repair scheduling
values.description: Quickly scheduling repair work after detecting a corrupted repository copy.

values.label: Replica quarantine after write disagreement
values.description: Removes replicas that lose a write vote from service until repair restores agreement.

values.label: Replica catch-up load after withheld writes
values.description: Additional catch-up work caused when writes are withheld from a quiescing replica.

values.label: Lost progress from interrupted large-repository reads
values.description: Breaking a long read forces a restart and loses clone progress.

selected_clusters.name: Client Object Materialization
selected_clusters.description: How much repository object data is transferred and verified on the client?

relations.reading: Choices on Client Object Materialization affect the outcomes of Git Performance Capability Boundary
relations.rationale: Partial transfer and sparse working directories reduce client processing demands, shaping whether performance requires an external layer or core Git capabilities.

values.label: Complete-object clone
values.description: The conventional approach transfers current and historical objects and requires extensive client-side hash verification.

values.label: GVFS partial object transfer
values.description: GVFS transfers commits and trees initially and retrieves missing objects on demand, accepting greater central-server coupling.

values.label: Full-clone client materialization
values.description: Materializing the complete repository working tree instead of using a sparse working directory.

selected_clusters.name: Working-Tree Materialization
selected_clusters.description: Which tracked files and working-directory content are materialized on the client?

values.label: Cone-mode sparse checkout
values.description: Clients initially materialize only repository-root files and explicitly expand directories needed for a task.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem materialization
values.description: Defers populated working-tree materialization through filesystem virtualization instead of sparse-checkout.

values.label: Populated-file change detection cost
values.description: The high operational cost of detecting changes among populated working-directory files.

selected_clusters.name: Git Performance Capability Boundary
selected_clusters.description: Are large-repository performance capabilities supplied by external tooling or standard Git?

values.label: Scalar performance layer
values.description: Scalar supplies the performance capabilities currently needed by large repositories as an interim layer above core Git.

values.label: Core Git performance capabilities
values.description: Performance features are added directly to Git so repositories can eventually rely on the core client alone.

values.label: GVFS Protocol outside standard Git
values.description: Keeping the GVFS Protocol as a specialized Scalar or hosting extension rather than standard Git functionality.

values.label: Filesystem virtualization for large repositories
values.description: A virtualized filesystem supplies large-repository performance outside standard Git behavior.

values.label: Client and build-machine cache proxies
values.description: Caches colocated with users and build machines reduce latency, increase throughput, and relieve central-server load.

selected_clusters.name: Git Performance Integration and Compatibility
selected_clusters.description: How are performance tooling dependencies, defaults, versions, and diagnosis integrated with Git workflows?

values.label: Removal of Git management layers
values.description: The intended outcome is eliminating separate management layers by incorporating their useful capabilities into Git itself.

values.label: Compatibility-driven default deactivation
values.description: Leaving advanced Git performance features disabled by default to preserve compatibility, with automated or manual configuration required.

values.label: Custom Git version dependency
values.description: Client acceleration depends on a custom Git release rather than only the standard Git client.

values.label: Performance tracing and user-feedback diagnosis
values.description: Custom tracing combined with user feedback identifies client performance bottlenecks for subsequent engineering changes.

values.label: Disabled ahead-behind status calculation
values.description: Disables nonessential ahead-behind comparison during status inspection to reduce interactive command latency.

selected_clusters.name: Object Replication Representation
selected_clusters.description: Which Git object representation and distribution level are used when replicating objects across hosting infrastructure.

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile fan-out
values.description: Large packfiles are distributed without consensus because objects remain unreachable until the smaller reference transaction commits.

values.label: Compacted-data replication
values.description: Incoming Git data is compacted once and the compacted representation is replicated across nodes.

values.label: Distributed key-value Git object storage
values.description: Git objects are stored in a distributed key-value system, including DHT-backed implementations replacing normal packfiles.

values.label: Packfile-level object replication
values.description: Repository data is replicated using Git packfiles without distributing the Git implementation itself.

values.label: Git-level object distribution
values.description: The replication system distributes or modifies Git itself as the repository propagation mechanism.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Compaction Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How and where Git object data is compacted, repacked, and resource-managed across replicas.

values.label: Git compaction throughput bottleneck
values.description: At low WAL latency, local Git-data compaction becomes the throughput limiting factor.

values.label: Replica-wide concurrent compaction
values.description: Runs compaction concurrently for the same repository on multiple replicas.

values.label: Compaction resource concentration
values.description: Concentrates compaction CPU on the primary while increasing replica bandwidth consumption for compacted-pack distribution.

values.label: Pack-file handle pressure
values.description: Unbounded pack-file accumulation exhausts client file-handle capacity and harms repository operation.

values.label: Reduced pack count and storage footprint
values.description: Incremental maintenance reduces the number and total storage footprint of repository pack-files.

values.label: Periodic incremental repository compaction
values.description: Compacts accumulated loose objects and pack-files incrementally or periodically to control storage and lookup costs.

values.label: Multi-pack-index guided compaction
values.description: Uses multi-pack indexes to preserve lookup and safely replace or expire packs without full repository repacking.

values.label: Primary-only repository compaction
values.description: Assigns repository compaction to the primary replica while other replicas consume the resulting compacted data.

values.label: Replica-local repository repacking
values.description: Performs independent repository repacking on each replica rather than consuming a primary-produced compaction result.

values.label: Single-pack-file repacking
values.description: Rewrites all repository objects into one pack-file as a consolidated garbage-collection operation.

selected_clusters.name: Object Storage and Transfer Representation
selected_clusters.description: Which physical representation and traversal strategy serves Git objects to clients and hosting operations?

values.label: Packfile network interchange
values.description: Using packfiles as the protocol-level format for Git object transfer.

values.label: Size-minimizing packfile layout
values.description: Packfiles organize compressed objects by size minimization rather than DAG locality.

values.label: DAG-dependent Git object traversal
values.description: Git objects are retrieved through sequential commit, tree, parent, and file-pointer traversal.

values.label: Round-trip-intensive distributed object retrieval
values.description: Distributed storage requires a network round trip for each successive object in a DAG walk.

values.label: Poor clone performance
values.description: Distributed object storage combined with packfile transfer produces unacceptable clone performance.

values.label: Adequate normal Git-operation performance
values.description: The distributed object implementation performs adequately for ordinary Git operations.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Storage Placement
selected_clusters.description: Where are complete repositories placed across machines, disks, and local or remote fileservers?

values.label: Co-located local repository storage
values.description: Repositories reside on the same machine and local filesystem as the hosting application.

values.label: Distributed filesystem for Git data
values.description: Distributing repository storage through a filesystem layer while preserving ordinary Git access.

values.label: Centralized NFS repository storage
values.description: Storing all repositories on a centralized network filesystem.

values.label: Single on-disk repository behind an HTTP daemon
values.description: Serving one filesystem repository through an HTTP daemon as the simple hosting architecture.

values.label: Multi-disk multi-machine repository placement
values.description: Distributing repository data across disks and machines for parallel operations and failure tolerance.

values.label: Fast local NVMe Git repository
values.description: Complete Git repositories use local NVMe storage for fast random-read operations at scale.

values.label: Spokes repository replication
values.description: A hosting application architecture replaces filesystem-block duplication with application-level repository replication.

values.label: Distant replica placement
values.description: Replica copies are intentionally placed across physical or geographic distance to avoid co-location constraints.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Each repository resides on only one machine, leaving availability and busiest-repository performance unresolved.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Storage Access and Representation
selected_clusters.description: How do hosting applications access repository data through filesystems, RPC, caching, and storage abstractions?

values.label: Network-filesystem performance degradation
values.description: Slow Git behavior caused by network-filesystem access characteristics.

values.label: Network-filesystem correctness bugs
values.description: Git locking, tearing, reading, or syncing failures caused by network-filesystem semantics.

values.label: Packfile storage scalability limitation
values.description: Availability and scalability limits caused by large binary packfiles requiring filesystem management.

values.label: Filesystem-accessible packfile storage
values.description: Keeping compressed repository objects in packfiles accessible through a filesystem for Git operations.

values.label: RPC access to dedicated fileserver repositories
values.description: Applications access repositories on dedicated fileservers through remote procedure calls.

values.label: Whole-packfile local caching
values.description: A complete packfile is cached locally to make random Git object access performant.

values.label: JGit repository-storage abstraction
values.description: JGit abstracts normal repository storage so alternate object backends can replace on-disk packfiles.

values.label: Untransformed Git repository representation
values.description: Repositories remain in Git's native format rather than being transformed into an alternate storage representation.

selected_clusters.name: Hosting Application Scaling
selected_clusters.description: How the hosting application itself is deployed and scaled as usage grows.

values.label: Rails monolith deployment
values.description: Running the hosting application as one co-located Rails instance.

values.label: Horizontal Rails application scaling
values.description: Deploying additional Rails instances to scale application demand.

values.label: Integrated version-control hosting platform
values.description: A dedicated hosting platform combines reliability, performance, and scale capabilities for repository service operation.

values.label: Agent-driven repository workload growth
values.description: Software agents increase code, pull-request, and CI workloads that hosting must scale to serve.

values.label: Repository-service downtime productivity loss
values.description: Push, pull, or CI outages impose substantial developer and organizational productivity costs.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Placement Management
selected_clusters.description: How repository location and materialization are managed across hosting nodes.

values.label: Authoritative repository-location database
values.description: An external routing database records each repository and every hosting machine containing it.

values.label: Stateless repository placement
values.description: Repositories may reside on any eligible node without durable server-side placement state.

values.label: On-demand repository materialization
values.description: Recreating a missing local repository from the authoritative log when needed.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
values.description: Deriving expected repository nodes from repository identity and the current healthy-node set.

values.label: Repository copies as individually managed pets
values.description: Tracking and caring for each repository copy individually rather than treating copies as interchangeable capacity.

values.label: Tolerance for stale routing state
values.description: Allowing repository-to-node routing information to become stale because correctness survives rematerialization elsewhere.

values.label: Repository-location database availability dependency
values.description: Repository access depends on availability of the external location-routing service.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Read Routing
selected_clusters.description: How Git reads are routed among healthy, synchronized, and geographically distributed replicas.

values.label: Health-aware replica failover routing
values.description: Routing requests away from failed or degraded servers using application-level health signals.

values.label: Geographically closest synchronized replica routing
values.description: Serving reads from the nearest replica known to be synchronized.

values.label: Geo-replicated Git read serving
values.description: Using geographically distributed replicas to serve Git reads near users.

values.label: Combined heartbeat and application-traffic failure detection
values.description: Using both heartbeats and real Git requests to detect server failure.

values.label: Application-level health validation
values.description: Validating server health through real authenticated Git operations rather than no-op checks alone.

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: Marking a node offline only after three consecutive failed requests.

values.label: Non-voting geo-replicated hosts
values.description: Keeping geographically replicated read hosts outside the push-voting quorum.

values.label: Live-traffic-based failure detection
values.description: Using live application traffic to determine server availability for routing decisions.

values.label: Operation-failure-based node detection
values.description: Failed repository operations, rather than heartbeat failure, identify unavailable or overloaded nodes.

values.label: Advisory replica offline marking
values.description: Repeated failures lower a replica's preference without removing its fallback availability.

values.label: Heartbeat-based primary failure detection
values.description: Heartbeats serve as the primary mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views
values.description: Each application server independently records which file servers appear offline.

values.label: Cross-server failure-correlation diagnosis
values.description: Correlated offline reports distinguish file-server faults from application-server faults.

values.label: RPC failover-pattern monitoring
values.description: Aggregate RPC redirection patterns expose misbehaving servers operationally.

values.label: Faster geographically local Git transfers
values.description: Reduced transfer distance and faster Git reads for users near synchronized replicas.

values.label: False-positive node isolation
values.description: Healthy nodes can be incorrectly isolated after random consecutive request failures.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Workflow Distribution
selected_clusters.description: Whether repository hosting and development follow distributed or centralized workflow and hosting models.

values.label: Distributed version-control architecture
values.description: Retaining distributed repository capabilities as the architectural model.

values.label: Decentralized maintainer workflow
values.description: Supporting many maintainers and decentralized development through distributed repositories.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting model
values.description: Using a centralized host for ordinary projects and company workflows.

values.label: Distributed-model operational hindrance
values.description: Operational friction arising when distributed capabilities serve predominantly centralized workflows.

values.label: Large-scale Git hosting difficulty
values.description: Operational difficulty of hosting Git repositories at large scale.

selected_clusters.name: Client Index Management
selected_clusters.description: How clients represent and optimize tracked-path metadata for large repositories.

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: Maintaining an index entry for every tracked path to support core Git operations.

values.label: Single-file index storage
values.description: Reading and writing the client index as one filesystem file using streaming I/O.

values.label: Updated index format
values.description: Using a newer index representation to reduce large-index storage and I/O costs.

values.label: Untracked cache
values.description: Enabling cached untracked-file information to reduce large working-directory processing.

values.label: Index-format size reduction
values.description: Reduced index storage and I/O resulting from the updated index representation.

values.label: Low per-entry index processing time
values.description: Low average processing cost per index entry despite a large absolute index.

selected_clusters.name: Working-Tree Change Detection
selected_clusters.description: How clients identify changed working-tree paths without scanning all populated files.

values.label: Filesystem event monitoring
values.description: Using Git fsmonitor and an event-monitoring tool to identify changed paths.

values.label: Modified-path-only inspection
values.description: Restricting index and cache work to paths reported as modified.

values.label: Watchman-based filesystem watching
values.description: Uses the general Watchman watcher rather than a Git-aware watcher for working-tree change detection.

values.label: Modified-size-dependent command work
values.description: Command work scales with the number of differing, untracked, or ignored paths.

values.label: Reduced Git status latency
values.description: Lower status-command latency when filesystem monitoring avoids scanning unchanged populated files.

selected_clusters.name: Client Background Synchronization
selected_clusters.description: How clients synchronize remote objects and references while preserving foreground user-visible state.

values.label: Background object fetch with hidden refs
values.description: Fetching remote objects periodically into a hidden reference namespace without changing normal tracking refs.

values.label: Foreground user-visible ref updates
values.description: Applying remote-tracking and local reference updates through explicit foreground fetches.

selected_clusters.name: Client Repository Maintenance Execution
selected_clusters.description: How client repository maintenance is activated, scheduled, executed, and paused.

values.label: Explicit repository registration
values.description: Users explicitly register repositories to activate client configuration and maintenance.

values.label: Scheduled background maintenance
values.description: Registered repositories receive automatic background maintenance without foreground user execution.

values.label: Foreground maintenance execution
values.description: Users explicitly run unified or individual maintenance tasks on demand.

values.label: Maintenance pause and unregister controls
values.description: Users can pause or unregister repositories to stop future automatic maintenance.

values.label: Automatic clone enlistment registration
values.description: Cloning automatically registers the new enlistment for recommended configuration and maintenance.

values.label: Synchronous end-of-command maintenance
values.description: Repository maintenance runs synchronously at interactive command completion.

values.label: Disabled foreground automatic garbage collection
values.description: Disables command-triggered automatic garbage collection so routine Git commands avoid expensive maintenance pauses.

values.label: Foreground periodic garbage collection
values.description: Runs periodic garbage collection in the foreground during ordinary repository work.

values.label: Asynchronous incremental commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Updating reachable commit-graph data asynchronously with split incremental files.

values.label: Interactive maintenance blocking
values.description: Expensive maintenance blocks foreground Git commands and user interaction.

values.label: Client resource exhaustion during maintenance
values.description: Large maintenance rewrites consume enough CPU and memory to stall the client system.

values.label: Performance decay after maintenance suppression
values.description: Suppressing automatic maintenance allows accumulated objects to degrade Git performance over time.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are not cleanly separated for the large-scale hosting use case. Repository Replica Count (30) overlaps Replica Write Durability (35): values 35.5 "Sub-three replica allocation" and 35.14 "Minimum two-replica write commitment" answer how many replicas are required, so move them to 30 while retaining quorum and acknowledgement guarantees in 35. Replica Commit Coordination (34) also overlaps both durability and replication mechanism: move 34.9 "Synchronous replica commitment" to 35 and move 34.15 "S3-backed WAL synchronization and source of truth" and 34.16 "WAL-first replica synchronization" to Repository Replication Mechanism (28). Repository Storage Placement (25) and Repository Placement Management (10) partially ask the same placement question; keep physical location alternatives such as 25.5 and 25.8 in 25, and keep routing/materialization policies such as 10.3 and 10.4 in 10. Most client dimensions, such as object materialization (19) versus working-tree materialization (20), and index management (13) versus change detection (14), do ask distinct questions, but the replica-related overlap is substantial.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have explicit decision questions and specific, distinguishable values relevant to scaling very large repositories and many users across servers and clients. The main revisions are: rename dimension 3, "Reference-State Integrity Verification," and replace its vague "axis of variation" description with a direct question about how reference divergence is detected and verification throughput is sustained; move value 19.3, "Full-clone client materialization," to dimension 20, "Working-Tree Materialization," because it describes the working tree rather than how much object data is transferred; move value 21.5, "Client and build-machine cache proxies," out of dimension 21, "Git Performance Capability Boundary," because it describes caching placement rather than whether capabilities belong in external tooling or core Git; and revise value 22.1, "Removal of Git management layers," so its label and description state an architectural option rather than an intended outcome. These changes would remove the clearest dimension/value mismatches without requiring additional content.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the major decision areas for scaling Git hosting and clients: application scaling (9), storage placement and access (25, 26), replication and durability (28, 30, 34, 35), routing and failure handling (11, 17, 18), large-repository object and compaction strategies (24, 32, 33), and client materialization and performance (13–16, 19–22). Nearly every dimension has multiple accepted, rejected, or mixed candidate decisions rather than only outcomes. The main residual weakness is that some narrow dimensions, especially Client Background Synchronization (15), Client Object Materialization (19), and Working-Tree Materialization (20), have only two candidate decisions; consolidate these with adjacent client dimensions where appropriate, such as merging 19 and 20 or 15 and 16, while retaining at least two candidates in each resulting dimension.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy is strongly aligned with the use case: dimensions cover server-side replication, coordination, durability, storage, routing, repair, compaction, and failure handling for many repositories and users, plus client-side materialization, indexing, change detection, caching, and maintenance for very large repositories. Dimension 12, "Repository Workflow Distribution," is tangential because distributed versus centralized development workflow is an operating-model choice rather than an architectural decision for scaling hosting servers or clients; drop dimension 12. The remaining dimensions are within the requested subject, lifecycle, and decision scope.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Most dimensions use specific architectural decisions and alternatives, but several values act as generic catch-all outcomes or optimizations. In dimension 12, values 12.4 "Distributed-model operational hindrance" and 12.5 "Large-scale Git hosting difficulty" broadly bundle unspecified problems; drop them or reorganize them into the concrete hosting and workflow decisions already represented elsewhere. In dimension 29, 29.5 "Read-preserving reference-update optimization" and 29.8 "Distributed reference-update performance optimization" are similarly nonspecific; drop these broad buckets and retain the concrete scheduling, batching, and latency values such as 29.1–29.4 and 29.9–29.11.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy broadly represents server- and client-side scaling decisions and uses accepted, rejected, mixed, and outcome statuses appropriately. However, several structural issues violate the one-decision-point rule: dimension 34, "Replica Commit Coordination," bundles commit protocol, locking, reference transactions, WAL synchronization, and repository-primary choices; split it into separate commit-protocol and reference/WAL-coordination dimensions using the existing values. Dimension 16, "Client Repository Maintenance Execution," combines activation, scheduling, execution, and pause/unregister decisions; split those into separate questions. Value 19.3, "Full-clone client materialization," answers the working-tree materialization decision rather than object transfer and should move to dimension 20. Value 21.5, "Client and build-machine cache proxies," is a caching/placement decision rather than an answer to the external-tooling-versus-core-Git boundary; move it to the existing storage/access dimension 26. Dimensions 28 and 34 also duplicate WAL-related replication content: move 28.7–28.9 into the WAL/coordination decision rather than treating provenance and compaction events as alternatives to the replication mechanism.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy has substantial relevant coverage for scaling Git across hosting servers and clients, and many dimensions have at least two candidate decisions with outcomes separated, such as 3 Reference-State Integrity Verification, 20 Working-Tree Materialization, and 30 Repository Replica Count. However, several dimensions combine distinct decision questions, which is a major violation of the design-space format. Split 34 Replica Commit Coordination into commit/locking protocol versus WAL/source-of-truth persistence, and move 34.14 to 30 Repository Replica Count. Split 35 Replica Write Durability into write admission/acknowledgement versus durability and rollback guarantees. Split 11 Repository Read Routing into replica-selection policy versus failure detection and operational diagnosis. Split 16 Client Repository Maintenance Execution into registration/lifecycle control versus scheduling and execution policy. Split 21 Git Performance Capability Boundary into capability ownership (21.1-21.3) versus client mechanisms such as virtualization and caching (21.4-21.5). These changes preserve existing values while ensuring each resulting decision point has at least two candidate decisions; otherwise, the current broad groupings answer multiple questions despite the use case's distinct server-scale and client-scale concerns.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Although all values use valid status labels, several values violate the status semantics. In dimension 19, "Complete-object clone" (19.1) is an alternative but is marked outcome, while "Full-clone client materialization" (19.3) overlaps it with accepted status; consolidate or distinguish them and classify the alternative consistently. In dimension 25, "Single-machine repository placement" (25.9) is a rejected placement option, not an outcome; reclassify it. In dimension 33, "Replica-wide concurrent compaction" (33.2) describes a compaction alternative but is marked outcome; reclassify it as a candidate decision. Multiple mixed values are described as settled choices, including 30.3, 17.3, and 3.2 as rejected, and 19.2, 25.7, 25.8, and 16.7 as adopted; revise their descriptions to explicitly reflect disagreement or change their status. Dimension 34 also has mixed 34.3 described as an adopted authoritative source, requiring the same correction.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under at least one taxonomy dimension; no passage ids are unplaceable. Examples include Scalar configuration and Git-versus-Scalar integration in dimensions 21–22 (s04_p01), partial and sparse checkout in dimensions 19–20 (s04_p02, s05_p04), background maintenance and fetch in dimensions 15–16 (s05_p09, s05_p11), replication and quorum decisions in dimensions 28, 30, 34, and 35 (s02_p01, s02_p03, s03_p02), and quiesced rolling maintenance in dimension 17 (s03_p07, s03_p08). Background-only material such as introductions is correctly irrelevant under the evaluation steps.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: Most adopted and rejected options are named, including sparse checkout (20.1), background fetch and hidden refs (15.1), commit-graph and incremental maintenance (16.9), multi-pack indexes (33.7), quiesced rolling reboots (17.1), quorum writes (35.7), and the replication and transaction mechanisms in s01–s03. Missing options are: add a value for standard Git partial clone to dimension 19, supported by s04_p01 and s04_p02; add a value for placing the clone under a src subdirectory to dimension 20 or a new repository-layout dimension, supported by s04_p02 and s05_p04; add a controlled server-retirement option that keeps the retiring server available while replica repairs run to dimension 17 or 18, supported by s03_p09; and add rendezvous-ranked primary selection/fallback to dimension 34, supported by s01_p11.

criteria.name: Value exclusivity
criteria.description: Each system (source) adopts one value per dimension: the values of a dimension are alternatives, not features used together. Deterministic: computed from the evidence, without a judge.
criteria.reason:
- Dimension 28 'Repository Replication Mechanism': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 28.1 'Application-level repository replication' and 28.3 'All-replica update replication' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p02, s01_p06, s01_p07).
- Dimension 35 'Replica Write Durability': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 35.7 'Quorum-based push acceptance' and 35.8 'Durable push acknowledgement' are adopted together by s01, s03 (passages s01_p09, s01_p10, s01_p15).
- Dimension 3 'Reference-State Integrity Verification': 2 of 2 sources adopt several of its values. Values 3.1 'Incremental XOR reference checksum' and 3.3 'Per-update checksum verification' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p09, s02_p05).
- Dimension 18 'Replica Lifecycle and Repair': 2 of 2 sources adopt several of its values. Values 18.1 'Idle replica garbage collection' and 18.2 'Rapid repository repair scheduling' are adopted together by s01, s03 (passages s01_p09, s01_p12, s03_p01).
Values one source uses together are not alternatives. Split such a dimension into the questions its values answer (every part keeps at least two candidate decisions), move a value to the existing dimension whose question it answers, or merge two values that are the same option.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: The dimensions mostly ask distinct questions: replica allocation (1), synchronization and propagation (2), integrity verification (3), maintenance (4), client materialization (5), and Git integration boundary (6). The main overlap is between 1, Repository Replica Capacity, and 2, Replica Synchronization Architecture: value 2.4, Replica-count scaling under three-phase commit, is primarily about expanding the replica set and overlaps with 1.3, Replica-count expansion for capacity. Move 2.4 to dimension 1 (or otherwise keep replica-count alternatives there) so dimension 2 contains only propagation and coordination choices. No other clear same-question pair requires merging.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have clear names and descriptions, and the values are generally distinguishable: for example, dimension 2 separates coordinated reference commits, S3-backed WAL propagation, and unsynchronized packfile distribution, while dimension 4 clearly distinguishes rolling reboots, quiescence, and rack-scoped maintenance. The main weakness is dimension 1: "Repository Replica Capacity" combines overlapping choices, since demand-scaled replica elasticity (1.2) and replica-count expansion for capacity (1.3) are difficult to distinguish; rename the dimension to explicitly ask how replica counts and lifecycles are allocated, and clarify or consolidate those values. Dimension 5's "Client Repository Materialization" does not naturally cover the cache-placement choice in 5.4; rename the dimension to include client-side caching and access, or move 5.4 under the existing dimension whose question covers performance integration. In dimension 6, 6.2 "Core Git performance capabilities" and 6.3 "Removal of Git management layers" substantially repeat the same alternative and should be merged or one should be repositioned as the resulting effect.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the main server and client scaling decision areas with multiple alternatives: replica allocation in dimension 1, synchronization in dimension 2, integrity verification in dimension 3, maintenance in dimension 4, and client materialization and caching in dimension 5. Dimension 6 also presents alternatives for placing performance capabilities in Scalar versus core Git. The main shortcoming is that repository serving and storage-placement choices for very many repositories are not an explicit decision point; reorganize the existing storage-related alternatives, especially 1.1-1.5 and 5.4, into a clearly named decision dimension with at least two candidate options. Also, dimension 3 has only two actual candidate decisions (3.1 and 3.2), while 3.3 largely repeats verification rather than providing a distinct alternative, so move or merge 3.3 with the checksum decision rather than treating it as a separate choice.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.

Dimension 4, "Server Maintenance Strategy," combines reboot approach, quiescence, and rack maintenance domains; fold 4.3 and 4.4 into the rolling-reboot option 4.1 or otherwise narrow the dimension. criteria.reason: Several dimensions are broad topic groupings rather than single decision points for the stated server/client scale use case. Dimension 1 (Repository Replica Capacity) mixes replica-count allocation (1.1–1.4) with replica lifecycle garbage collection (1.5); move 1.5 to an existing lifecycle decision or remove it rather than creating a one-option dimension. Dimension 2 (Replica Synchronization Architecture) mixes reference synchronization, packfile fan-out (2.3), and replica-count scaling (2.4); move 2.4 to dimension 1 and reorganize 2.3 with an existing object-distribution decision. Dimension 4 (Server Maintenance Strategy) combines reboot scheduling, quiescence, rack domains, and unplanned failure, so its values answer multiple questions; split only where each resulting decision retains at least two candidates, otherwise move the odd values. Dimension 5 (Client Repository Materialization) combines object transfer (5.1–5.2), sparse checkout (5.3), and caching (5.4), which should be merged into existing decision points answering those separate questions; 5.1 is also a candidate approach but is incorrectly marked as an outcome. Dimension 3 mostly has a coherent checksum-method choice, though 3.3 is verification cadence rather than algorithm choice. Dimension 6 has two valid alternatives (6.1–6.2), but 6.3 explicitly describes an outcome and should be marked accordingly.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: Most decision-bearing passages map to the replica, synchronization, maintenance, client materialization, or Git-integration dimensions. The passages that cannot be placed are s02_p02 (placing replicas across distant locations and managing latency), s02_p06 (coalescing bookkeeping updates and prioritizing user updates, plus geo-replica read routing), s01_p05 (choosing RPC-based dedicated fileservers over distributed filesystems), s01_p03 (choosing whether to distribute the filesystem, packfiles, or Git itself), and s01_p04 (rejecting NFS and other distributed-filesystem designs). Add a storage-distribution architecture dimension with values for distributed filesystem, distributed packfiles, and RPC/dedicated-fileserver storage, supported by s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05; add a replica-placement value or dimension for geographically distant replicas and nearest-replica reads, supported by s02_p02 and s02_p06; and add a value to dimension 2, Replica Synchronization Architecture, for coalesced bookkeeping transactions with user-update priority, supported by s02_p06.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers several explicit Spokes choices, including fixed three-replica allocation (1.1), three-phase commit (2.1), rolling reboots, quiescence, rack maintenance, unplugging, cone-mode sparse checkout (5.3), and the Scalar/core-Git boundary. However, many adopted or rejected options in the passages are unnamed. Add values to dimension 6, "Git Performance Integration Boundary," for Scalar's index compression, hourly background fetch, background commit-graph and multi-pack-index maintenance, built-in filesystem monitor, and incremental background maintenance, supported by s04_p02, s05_p09, s05_p11, and s05_p12. Add to dimension 5, "Client Repository Materialization," the standard Git partial-clone option (distinct from GVFS) and the /src layout for separating build artifacts, supported by s04_p01, s04_p02, and s05_p04. Add to dimension 2, "Replica Synchronization Architecture," values for geographically distant replicas, nearest-replica read routing, non-voting geo replicas, and coalescing/prioritizing user updates, supported by s02_p01, s02_p02, and s02_p06. Add to dimension 2 the rejected distributed-filesystem/block-level replication alternatives and the adopted dedicated-fileserver RPC approach, supported by s01_p03, s01_p04, s01_p05, and s02_p01. Add to dimension 1 or 2 values for rendezvous-hash repository placement and arbitrary-server primary selection, supported by s01_p11; dimension 4 also lacks the explicit choice to continue writes during quiescence and to retain a retiring server while repairs proceed, supported by s03_p07 and s03_p09.

criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions, such as client materialization (5), change detection (14), maintenance execution (16), and read routing (11), but several server-side dimensions overlap. Dimension 1, "Repository Replica Allocation," contains allocation decisions that belong in dimension 2, "Replica Synchronization Architecture": move 2.6 "Sub-three replica allocation" to dimension 1 and move 1.6 "Replica-count scaling under three-phase commit" to dimension 2. Dimension 2 also overlaps directly with dimension 3, "Reference-State Integrity Verification," because 2.7 "Per-update checksum verification" answers the checksum-verification question; move it to dimension 3. Finally, dimension 2 overlaps dimension 7, "Repository Object Distribution," through object-replication values such as 2.20, 2.21, 2.22, 2.23, and 2.30; move those values to dimension 7 while retaining WAL, coordination, and reference-synchronization choices in dimension 2.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions state a recognizable question and most values have detailed, distinguishable descriptions for server- and client-side scaling. However, dimension 10 "Repository Placement Management" contains near-duplicate values 10.1 "Authoritative repository-location database" and 10.8 "Centralized repository-location database"; rename them to explicitly distinguish external routing authority from a centralized relational table, or merge their descriptions. Dimension 8 "Repository Storage Access Architecture" similarly has overlapping 8.1 "Co-located local repository storage" and 8.10 "Fast local NVMe Git repository"; rename them to emphasize application/storage co-location versus the storage medium. Dimension 5 has near-duplicate concepts in 5.1 "Complete-object clone" and 5.6 "Full-clone client materialization"; make the former specifically about transferred object history and the latter specifically about working-tree population. Dimension 11 has several closely overlapping health-detection values—11.5, 11.6, 11.10, and 11.11—so revise their labels to clearly separate signals used, validation method, and routing consequence. Dimension 2 "Replica Synchronization Architecture" also spans WAL durability, commit coordination, reference bookkeeping, and Git/rsync replication; rename it to state this broader range or reorganize the existing values into more explicitly named subtopics.

Dimension 2, "Replica Synchronization Architecture," mixes synchronization protocol, WAL durability, reference-update optimization, replication layer, quorum behavior, and publication semantics; split it into separate decision questions and move checksum-related value 2.7 to dimension 3. Dimension 4, "Server Maintenance Strategy," combines reboot policy, quiescence behavior, replica garbage collection, repair scheduling, and failure isolation; separate those decision groups. Dimension 5, "Client Repository Materialization," combines object transfer, sparse working-tree selection, and caching; reorganize values 5.1–5.5, 5.3/5.6, and 5.4 under distinct decision questions. Dimension 11, "Repository Read Routing," combines replica-selection policy (11.1–11.4, 11.9) with failure-detection and health-marking mechanisms (11.5–11.16); separate those alternatives. These are structural one-decision violations, not shortcomings about missing rationale or use-case coverage.

Split 7 (Repository Object Distribution) into object replication/compaction and object storage or transfer representation. Split 8 (Repository Storage Access Architecture) into repository placement/access and object-storage backend decisions. criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many overlapping decision questions. Dimension 1, "Repository Replica Allocation," mixes replica-count allocation with coordination mechanisms and durability outcomes: move 1.6 "Replica-count scaling under three-phase commit" and 1.10 "Push unavailability after quorum loss" to dimension 27, "Replica Coordination and Durability," while retaining allocation and placement values in 1. Dimensions 27 and 28 also overlap on replication protocol and WAL synchronization; move protocol/commit choices such as 28.1, 28.2, and 28.7 to 27, or keep them in 28 only when they describe propagation mechanism rather than consistency or acceptance. Dimensions 23, 24, and 26 repeatedly address packfiles and Git object representation; move transfer-format values such as 24.1 and 24.2 to the representation dimension that asks that question, leaving 23 focused on replication/compaction and 26 on access. Dimension 19, "Client Object Materialization," includes 19.4 "Full-clone client materialization," which answers dimension 20, "Working-Tree Materialization," and should be moved there. Dimension 10, "Repository Placement Management," and dimension 11, "Repository Read Routing," also share routing concepts; keep node assignment and materialization in 10 and move read-selection/failover values such as 10.4 "Rendezvous-hashed repository routing" to 11 only if they describe serving reads rather than placement.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions clearly state a decision question and their values are often distinguishable, such as client change detection (14), background synchronization (15), and repository storage placement (25), covering both hosting servers and large-repository clients. However, several descriptions and values remain ambiguous: 10.1 "Authoritative repository-location database" and 10.8 "Centralized repository-location database" are effectively indistinguishable; rename or merge them to make the accepted and rejected alternatives materially different. In dimension 1, 1.2 "Demand-scaled replica elasticity" and 1.7 "Arbitrary replica expansion for read scaling" overlap; rename 1.7 to explicitly describe read-only scaling or merge it with 1.2. Dimension 27 contains overlapping coordination choices, especially 27.1 "Three-phase coordinated commit," 27.7 "Quorum-based push acceptance," and 27.20 "Synchronous replica commitment"; rewrite their labels/descriptions to distinguish protocol, quorum rule, and acknowledgement condition. Value 20.2 "Client and build-machine cache proxies" does not answer the working-tree materialization question in dimension 20; move it to the existing client object-materialization dimension or otherwise align its description with that dimension. Finally, 11.5 "Combined heartbeat and application-traffic failure detection" and 11.10 "Live-traffic-based failure detection" substantially overlap; merge them or make one explicitly the combined mechanism and the other a distinct fallback policy.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the major decision areas implied by scaling Git hosting for many repositories and users: server placement and replication (25, 26, 28), coordination and durability (27), routing and failover (10, 11, 17, 18), object storage and compaction (23, 24), application scaling (9), and client-side materialization and maintenance (13–16, 19–22). Each area has multiple candidate decisions with accepted or rejected alternatives—for example, dimension 25 contrasts local NVMe, multi-machine placement, distributed filesystems, and NFS, while dimension 19 contrasts complete cloning with GVFS partial transfer. No major use-case area is left without a decision point containing several candidates, so there is no shortcoming to fix under this criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment

criteria.reason: Nearly all dimensions are in scope for making Git work at scale across hosting servers and clients, including replication, storage placement, read routing, failure repair, object compaction, client materialization, indexing, change detection, and maintenance. Dimension 12, "Repository Workflow Distribution," is the main tangential item: its centralized/decentralized workflow choices and outcomes describe usage and organizational models rather than a concrete server/client scaling decision. Drop dimension 12 to keep the taxonomy focused on architectural mechanisms for very many repositories, very large repositories, and very many users.

criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many relevant decisions, but several dimensions mix multiple decision points or treat subtopics as alternatives. Split 27, "Replica Coordination and Durability," into separate commit-coordination and durability/write-acceptance questions; values such as 27.24–27.27 describe reference-transaction mechanics rather than alternatives to the whole dimension. Split 1, "Repository Replica Allocation," so replica-count/scaling values remain together and move placement values 1.11 and 1.12 to 25, "Repository Storage Placement." Split 23, "Object Replication and Compaction," into replication representation (23.1, 23.2, 23.5, 23.6) and compaction strategy (23.7–23.15). In 20, "Working-Tree Materialization," move 20.2, "Client and build-machine cache proxies," because it is a caching decision rather than a materialization option. criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many dimensions with multiple accepted/rejected alternatives and explicitly marked outcomes, covering both hosting and client concerns for large-scale repositories. However, several major dimensions combine distinct decision questions. Dimension 27, "Replica Coordination and Durability," mixes commit protocol, quorum/write acceptance, locking, validation, acknowledgement, and consistency policy; split these only into groups that each retain at least two candidate decisions, moving replication-specific values to 28 and checksum-related values to 3. Dimension 1, "Repository Replica Allocation," combines replica-count strategy with physical placement; split allocation from placement, since each has at least two candidates. Dimension 28, "Repository Replication Mechanism," mixes WAL/source-of-truth, propagation mechanisms, repair/history, and compaction; move compaction values to 23 and verification values to 3, and split the remaining groups only where each has two candidates. Dimension 11, "Repository Read Routing," combines routing choices with failure detection and operational diagnosis; split routing from failure detection/diagnosis, with each resulting dimension retaining at least two candidates. Dimensions 19 and 20 also mix object transfer, working-tree materialization, and caching; move 19.4 to 20, move the cache-proxy value to the decision point whose question it answers, and merge any resulting singleton dimension into its sibling rather than leaving fewer than two candidates.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling

In dimension 22, 22.1 "Removal of Git management layers" is explicitly described as an outcome but marked accepted; mark it as an outcome or rewrite it as the adopted decision. In dimension 23, 23.11 "Replica-wide concurrent compaction" is a decision alternative, not an outcome; reclassify it or reorganize it with the compaction alternatives. In dimension 25, 25.7 "Single-machine repository placement" is phrased as a candidate placement alternative but marked outcome; reclassify it or retain only its consequence as the outcome. In dimension 10, 10.1 and 10.8 both describe an authoritative centralized repository-location database but have conflicting accepted and rejected statuses; merge them or distinguish their content so one candidate is not repeated.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are not cleanly separated for the large-scale hosting use case. Repository Replica Count (30) overlaps Replica Write Durability (35): values 35.5 "Sub-three replica allocation" and 35.14 "Minimum two-replica write commitment" answer how many replicas are required, so move them to 30 while retaining quorum and acknowledgement guarantees in 35. Replica Commit Coordination (34) also overlaps both durability and replication mechanism: move 34.9 "Synchronous replica commitment" to 35 and move 34.15 "S3-backed WAL synchronization and source of truth" and 34.16 "WAL-first replica synchronization" to Repository Replication Mechanism (28). criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have explicit decision questions and specific, distinguishable values relevant to scaling very large repositories and many users across servers and clients. The main revisions are: rename dimension 3, "Reference-State Integrity Verification," and replace its vague "axis of variation" description with a direct question about how reference divergence is detected and verification throughput is sustained; move value 19.3, "Full-clone client materialization," to dimension 20, "Working-Tree Materialization," because it describes the working tree rather than how much object data is transferred; move value 21.5, "Client and build-machine cache proxies," out of dimension 21, "Git Performance Capability Boundary," because it describes caching placement rather than whether capabilities belong in external tooling or core Git; and revise value 22.1, "Removal of Git management layers," so its label and description state an architectural option rather than an intended outcome. These changes would remove the clearest dimension/value mismatches without requiring additional content.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the major decision areas for scaling Git hosting and clients: application scaling (9), storage placement and access (25, 26), replication and durability (28, 30, 34, 35), routing and failure handling (11, 17, 18), large-repository object and compaction strategies (24, 32, 33), and client materialization and performance (13–16, 19–22). In dimension 29, 29.5 "Read-preserving reference-update optimization" and 29.8 "Distributed reference-update performance optimization" are similarly nonspecific; drop these broad buckets and retain the concrete scheduling, batching, and latency values such as 29.1–29.4 and 29.9–29.11.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy broadly represents server- and client-side scaling decisions and uses accepted, rejected, mixed, and outcome statuses appropriately. However, several structural issues violate the one-decision-point rule: dimension 34, "Replica Commit Coordination," bundles commit protocol, locking, reference transactions, WAL synchronization, and repository-primary choices; split it into separate commit-protocol and reference/WAL-coordination dimensions using the existing values. Dimension 16, "Client Repository Maintenance Execution," combines activation, scheduling, execution, and pause/unregister decisions; split those into separate questions. Value 19.3, "Full-clone client materialization," answers the working-tree materialization decision rather than object transfer and should move to dimension 20. Value 21.5, "Client and build-machine cache proxies," is a caching/placement decision rather than an answer to the external-tooling-versus-core-Git boundary; move it to the existing storage/access dimension 26. Dimensions 28 and 34 also duplicate WAL-related replication content: move 28.7–28.9 into the WAL/coordination decision rather than treating provenance and compaction events as alternatives to the replication mechanism.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. criteria.reason: The taxonomy has substantial relevant coverage for scaling Git across hosting servers and clients, and many dimensions have at least two candidate decisions with outcomes separated, such as 3 Reference-State Integrity Verification, 20 Working-Tree Materialization, and 30 Repository Replica Count. However, several dimensions combine distinct decision questions, which is a major violation of the design-space format. Split 34 Replica Commit Coordination into commit/locking protocol versus WAL/source-of-truth persistence, and move 34.14 to 30 Repository Replica Count. Split 35 Replica Write Durability into write admission/acknowledgement versus durability and rollback guarantees. Split 11 Repository Read Routing into replica-selection policy versus failure detection and operational diagnosis. Split 16 Client Repository Maintenance Execution into registration/lifecycle control versus scheduling and execution policy. Split 21 Git Performance Capability Boundary into capability ownership (21.1-21.3) versus client mechanisms such as virtualization and caching (21.4-21.5). These changes preserve existing values while ensuring each resulting decision point has at least two candidate decisions; otherwise, the current broad groupings answer multiple questions despite the use case's distinct server-scale and client-scale concerns.
